'''Watercress''' or '''yellowcress''' ('''''Nasturtium officinale''''') is a species of [[aquatic plant|aquatic]] flowering plant in the cabbage family, [[Brassicaceae]].

Watercress is a rapidly growing [[perennial]] plant native to Eurasia. It is one of the oldest known [[leaf vegetable]]s consumed by humans. Watercress and many of its relatives, such as [[garden cress]], [[Mustard plant|mustard]], [[radish]], and [[wasabi]], are noteworthy for their [[piquant]] flavors.

== Description ==
Watercress can grow up to {{Convert|60|cm}} in length.<ref name="tfb">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=63}}</ref> The stems are hollow and float in water. The leaf structure is [[Pinnate|pinnately compound]]. Small, white,<ref name="tfb" /> and green [[inflorescence]]s are produced in clusters and are frequently visited by insects, especially [[hoverflies]], such as ''[[Eristalis]]'' flies.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/plb.12328 |pmid=25754608 |title=Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers |journal=[[Plant Biology (journal)|Plant Biology]] |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=56–62 |year=2016 |last1=Van Der Kooi |first1=C. J. |last2=Pen |first2=I. |last3=Staal |first3=M. |last4=Stavenga |first4=D. G. |last5=Elzenga |first5=J. T. M. |url=https://pure.rug.nl/ws/files/78585910/Competition_for_pollinators_and_intra_communal_spectral_dissimilarity_of_flowers.pdf }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Watercress is listed in some sources as belonging to the genus ''[[Rorippa]]'', although molecular evidence shows those aquatic species with hollow stems are more closely related to ''[[Cardamine]]'' than ''Rorippa''.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.2307/3391978 |jstor=3391978 |title=Delimitation of the Genus Nasturtium (Brassicaceae) |journal=[[Novon]] |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=124–6 |year=1998 |last1=Al-Shehbaz |first1=Ihsan A. |last2=Price |first2=Robert A. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/24865 }}</ref> Despite the Latin name, watercress is not particularly closely related to the flowers popularly known as nasturtiums (''[[Tropaeolum majus]]''). ''T. majus'' belongs to the family [[Tropaeolum|Tropaeolaceae]], a [[sister taxon]] to the Brassicaceae within the order [[Brassicales]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fay |first1=Michael F. |last2=Christenhusz |first2=Maarten J.M. |title=Brassicales - an Order of Plants Characterised by Shared Chemistry |date=2010-09-14 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-8748.2010.01695.x |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |language=en |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=165–196 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-8748.2010.01695.x|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==

An aquatic [[vegetable]] or [[herb]], watercress has grown in many [[Temperate climate|temperate]] locations worldwide.<ref>{{Cite web| title= Plant of the Week: Watercress (''Nasturtium officinale'') |url= https://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/plant-of-the-week/nasturtium_officinale.shtml |first= Dave |last= Moore |website= fs.fed.us |publisher= US Forest Service, US Department of Agriculture |url-status= dead| archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20210406224734/https://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/plant-of-the-week/nasturtium_officinale.shtml | archivedate= 2021-04-06 |access-date=2026-05-08}}</ref>

Watercress was introduced into [[China]] through [[Hong Kong]] and [[Macao]] in the 1800s from Europe. Its cultivation also spread to highland areas in the tropical regions of Asia.<ref name="Cook's Guide">{{cite book |last1=Hutton |first1=Wendy |title=A Cook's Guide to Asian Vegetables |date=2004 |publisher=Periplus Editions |location= Singapore |isbn=0-7946-0078-6 |page=54}}</ref>

Clear fast-flowing [[chalk stream]]s are the primary natural habitat for wild watercress in the UK.<ref>{{harvnb|Mabey|1996|p=147}} "Water-cress was traditionally picked wild from the edges of fast-flowing streams, where it can grow in thick drifts...by the 19th century it was certainly under small-scale cultivation, especially in areas where there were clear [[chalk streams]], such as [[Wiltshire]] and the north [[Chilterns]]..."</ref> Many settlements in England are named after watercress, from [[Old English]] ''êacerse'', including [[Kersey, Suffolk|Kersey]], [[Kesgrave]], [[Kersal]], and [[Kershopefoot]].{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=147}}

== Ecology ==
In some regions, watercress is regarded as a [[weed]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Ecological-Risk-Screening-Summary-Watercress.pdf |title= Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) - Ecological Risk Screening Summary |author= Cao & Berent and CABI | website= fws.gov |date= 4 February 2019 |publisher= US Fish & Wildlife Service,  US Department of the Interior |page= 11 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20251112170249/https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Ecological-Risk-Screening-Summary-Watercress.pdf |archive-date= 12 November 2025 |access-date= 2026-05-08}}</ref> When introduced into non-native environments, watercress can have negative impacts on native species. With the introduction of watercress, the organic matter in the sediment increases which in turn attracts predatory macroinvertebrates that feed on other plants in the environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bergey |first=Elizabeth A. |date=2024-01-25 |title=The impacts of non-native watercress in Oklahoma spring ecosystems |journal= Aquatic Ecology |language=en |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=411–427 |doi=10.1007/s10452-023-10081-3 |issn=1573-5125 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Due to its fast-growing nature and [[invasive species]] status, ''N. officinale'' is prohibited in [[Illinois]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nasturtium officinale W.T. Aiton |url= https://nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/GreatLakes/FactSheet.aspx?Species_ID=229&State=&HUCNumber# |website= nas.er.usgs.gov |date=30 July 2019 |publisher=US Geological Survey |vauthors=Cao L, Berent L |access-date= 15 June 2022}}</ref>

Crops grown in the presence of [[manure]] can be an environment for [[parasite]]s such as the [[liver fluke]], ''[[Fasciola hepatica]]''.<ref>{{cite web |date=29 November 2013 |title=DPDx - Laboratory Identification of Parasitic Diseases of Public Health Concern: Fascioliasis |url=https://www.cdc.gov/dpdx/fascioliasis/index.html |publisher=US Centers for Disease Control}}</ref> Cultivated watercress has the advantage of being free of the liver fluke.{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=148}}

== Cultivation ==
[[File:WarnfordWatercress.jpg|thumb|upright=1.25|Watercress beds in [[Warnford]], Hampshire, England]]

Watercress cultivation is practical on both a large scale and a garden scale. Being semi-aquatic, watercress is well-suited to [[hydroponic]] cultivation, thriving best in water that is slightly [[alkaline]]. It is frequently produced around the headwaters of [[chalk stream]]s. In many local markets, the demand for hydroponically grown watercress exceeds supply, partly because cress leaves are unsuitable for distribution in dried form and can be stored fresh for only 2–3 days.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Long Does Fresh Watercress Last? |url=https://www.stilltasty.com/fooditems/index/18664#:~:text=To%20maximize%20the%20shelf%20life,3%20days%20in%20the%20refrigerator. |access-date=2022-06-16 |website=www.stilltasty.com}}</ref>

Also sold as [[Sprouting|sprouts]], the edible shoots are harvested days after germination. If unharvested, watercress can grow to a height of {{convert|50 to 120|cm|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}.

In the UK, watercress was first commercially cultivated in 1808 by the horticulturist [[William Bradbery]] along the [[River Ebbsfleet]] in [[Kent]]. Historically important areas of cultivation also included [[Hampshire]], [[Stamford, Lincolnshire|Stamford]] and [[Watercress Wildlife Site]] at [[St Albans]].{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=148}} Watercress is now grown in several counties, most notably Hampshire, [[Dorset]], [[Wiltshire]] and [[Hertfordshire]]. [[New Alresford]] in Hampshire is considered to be the nation's watercress capital.<ref>{{cite news |last=Peters |first=Rick |date=30 March 2010 |title=Seasonal food: watercress |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2010/mar/30/seasonal-food-watercress |access-date=15 December 2012 |newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref>

== Potential drug interaction ==
By inhibiting the [[cytochrome P450|cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2E1]], the [[phenethyl isothiocyanate]] within watercress may cause adverse [[drug interaction]]s in individuals taking certain medications, such as [[chlorzoxazone]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leclercq |first1=Isabelle |last2=Desager |first2=Jean-Pierre |last3=Horsmans |first3=Yves |year=1998 |title=Inhibition of chlorzoxazone metabolism, a clinical probe for CYP2E1, by a single ingestion of watercress |journal=Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics |volume=64 |issue=2 |pages=144–9 |doi=10.1016/S0009-9236(98)90147-3 |pmid=9728894 |s2cid=43863786}}</ref>

Raw watercress is 95% water, 1% [[carbohydrate]]s, 2% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and contains negligible [[fat]]. In a reference amount of {{cvt|100|g}}, raw watercress provides 11 [[calorie]]s of [[food energy]], and is a rich source (20% or more of the [[Daily Value]], DV) of [[vitamin K]] (208% DV) and [[vitamin C]] (48% DV), with moderate amounts (11–18% DV) of [[vitamin A]], [[manganese in biology|manganese]], and [[potassium in biology|potassium]].

=== Culinary ===
Watercress leaves, stems, and fruit can be eaten raw.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Benoliel |first=Doug |title=Northwest Foraging: The Classic Guide to Edible Plants of the Pacific Northwest |publisher=Skipstone |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-59485-366-1 |edition=Rev. and updated |location=Seattle, WA |page=161 |oclc=668195076}}</ref> In China watercress is often boiled alongside pork and traditional medicinal ingredients to make a wintertime [[Herbal tonic|tonic]] soup. In [[Vietnamese cuisine|Vietnam]] it is generally used raw as a component in salads.<ref name="Cook's Guide" />

The new tips of watercress leaves can be eaten raw or cooked,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Nyerges|first1=Christopher|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ|title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles|date=2016|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6}}</ref> although caution should be used when collecting these in the wild because of parasites such as ''[[giardia]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Blackwell|first=Laird R.|title=Great Basin Wildflowers: A Guide to Common Wildflowers of the High Deserts of Nevada, Utah, and Oregon (A Falcon Guide)|publisher=[[Morris Book Publishing, LLC]]|year=2006|isbn=0-7627-3805-7|edition=1st|location=Guilford, Conn.|page=196|oclc=61461560}}</ref>

As a [[cruciferous vegetable]], watercress contains [[isothiocyanate]]s that are partly destroyed by boiling, while the [[bioavailability]] of its [[carotenoid]]s is slightly increased by cooking. Steaming or [[microwave oven|microwave cooking]] retains these [[phytochemical]]s somewhat better than boiling.<ref name="Giall">{{cite journal|last1=Giallourou|first1=Natasa|last2=Oruna-Concha|first2=Maria Jose|last3=Harbourne|first3=Niamh|date=1 November 2016|title=Effects of domestic processing methods on the phytochemical content of watercress (''Nasturtium officinale'')|url=http://centaur.reading.ac.uk/65845/3/Manuscript_Revised%20watercress.pdf|journal=Food Chemistry|volume=212|pages=411–419|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2016.05.190|issn=0308-8146|pmid=27374550}}</ref>

=== Traditional uses ===
{{See also|Traditional medicine}}

[[Ancient Romans]] thought eating the plant would cure mental illness.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Lyle |first=Katie Letcher |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants, Mushrooms, Fruits, and Nuts: How to Find, Identify, and Cook Them |publisher=[[FalconGuides]] |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-59921-887-8 |edition=2nd |location=Guilford, CN |pages=34–35 |oclc=560560606 |orig-date=2004}}</ref> Twelfth-century mystic [[Hildegard of Bingen]] thought eating it steamed and drinking the water would cure jaundice or fever.<ref name=":0" /> Watercress was eaten by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Nyerges |first=Christopher |title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods |publisher=Falcon Guides |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3 |location=Guilford, CT |oclc=965922681}}</ref> Some Native Americans used it to treat [[kidney]] illnesses and [[constipation]], and it was thought by some to be an [[aphrodisiac]].<ref name=":0" /> Early [[African Americans]] used the plant as an [[abortifacient]]; it was believed to cause sterility as well.<ref name=":0" />

==In culture==
Hampshire's [[Watercress Line]] was named after the plant, a common cargo of that railway.{{sfn|Mabey|1996|p=148}}
